newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela cool on U.S.-proposed Africa peace force.
newsitem.headline: Mandela cool on U.S.-proposed Africa peace force.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela said on Saturday he could not support a U.S.-led proposal for an African intervention force, unless it was set up through the United Nations.
Mandela held talks with U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher on Saturday, focusing mainly on a U.S. initiative to convene an African Crisis Response Force of up to 10,000 troops.
The president was cautious in his response to the proposed force, saying: "My point of view is if this initiative is to succeed, it must have credibility.
"It (the initiative) must not come from one country. It should be the initiative of the United Nations. In such a case it would receive wide support," he told reporters after their discussions.
"I would like the whole process to come through the United Nations, including resources and equipment," he said when asked if he would accept U.S. funding for a rapid deployment force.
Mandela said South Africa might contribute troops to a peacekeeping force if it became essential.

"We are part of the United Nations and part of the OAU (Organisation of African Unity). If we are asked, and we have the capacity, we will discuss it in the government...with parliament. When it is absolutely necessary we would do so (contribute)."
Asked by reporters if he was disappointed at Mandela's cool response to the proposal, Christopher, who is on his first trip to Africa in four years, said he was not.
"This is exactly the sort of information we are looking for," he said, adding that the idea for an intervention force was not exclusively the preserve of the United States.

The proposal was being widely canvassed in the region, with the OAU and the United Nations, said Christopher, who arrived in South Africa from Tanzania for the fourth leg of a five-nation African tour.

"I assured the president that the United States would work closely with international organisations as well as countries in the region to try to develop this concept. With the crises coming onto the scene (in Africa) we need to be better prepared to deal with them," he told the joint briefing with Mandela.
The United States has undertaken to pay a quarter of the estimated $40 million cost of training a pan-African force and has pledged an additional $10 million.
Britain, Canada, Ireland and Belgium have also promised financial support for the plan.

Mandela has so far resisted a unilateral diplomatic role in peacemaking or a military role for South Africa's defence force, which is still merging the old army and the liberation forces it fought under apartheid.
The two also discussed the situations in Nigeria and Burundi, both under military rule, and the opposition of the United States to a second term for U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

"Our attitude in Africa, both in SADC (the Southern African Development Community) and the OAU, is to support Boutros Boutros-Ghali in seeking a second term. We know the difficulty which we are facing if we cannot get the United States on board on this issue," Mandela said.

Boutros-Ghali, the first secretary-general from the African continent, ends his five-year term on December 31 and the United States is trying to persuade members to dump him, for failing to give enough attention to restructuring the world body.
